lesson.title: Splitting a Sum Before You Integrate
lesson.summary: The sum rule for integration lets you integrate a sum of functions term by term, since ∫[f(x) + g(x)]dx = ∫f(x)dx + ∫g(x)dx.
lesson.body:
Most integrands you will meet in practice are not single terms like 3x^2 or 7; they are sums of several terms, like 3x^2 + 4x. Rather than inventing a new technique for every possible combination, integration offers a rule that lets you break a sum apart and handle each piece with tools you already have.

The sum rule states: ∫[f(x) + g(x)]dx = ∫f(x)dx + ∫g(x)dx. In words, the indefinite integral of a sum equals the sum of the indefinite integrals. This property is called linearity, and it exists because differentiation has the matching property: the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, d/dx[F(x) + G(x)] = F'(x) + G'(x). Since integration undoes differentiation, whatever splitting works for derivatives works in reverse for antiderivatives too.

Let's apply it to a full example: ∫(3x^2 + 4x)dx. Split the integrand into two pieces using the sum rule: ∫3x^2 dx + ∫4x dx. Integrate each piece using the power rule. For the first piece, ∫3x^2 dx = 3 · (x^3/3) = x^3. For the second piece, ∫4x dx = 4 · (x^2/2) = 2x^2. Combine the results and add a single constant of integration at the end: x^3 + 2x^2 + C.

Check the answer by differentiating the whole thing: d/dx[x^3 + 2x^2 + C] = 3x^2 + 4x + 0 = 3x^2 + 4x, which matches the original integrand exactly. Notice that even though we integrated two separate terms, we only wrote one C at the end, not one constant for each piece. That is because the sum of two arbitrary constants is itself just some arbitrary constant, so combining them into a single C at the very end is standard practice and keeps the general antiderivative in its simplest form.
